_comment: What CALL-E actually billed this account, read off the account's own usage page. This is a first-party observation and not a published price, so it is here rather than in statistics.json, which holds figures with a public URL a reader can open. A district must confirm its own pricing before relying on any of it. tests/test_observed_price.py fails if the README or the page quotes a different number, and tools/money_across_runs.py puts it beside the ceiling the run derives.

observed.account: the author's own CALL-E account, created for this hackathon
observed.surface: the Usage panel of the CALL-E dashboard, All countries, Date Range 2026-08-07 to 2026-09-07

what_it_supports: Every one of the ten rows on the usage panel is $0.05, and the period total of $0.65 divides by $0.05 exactly, so thirteen billable events were priced identically.
The durations on those rows run from 35 seconds to 1 minute 50, so the price did not move with the length of the call across that range.

Twelve of the thirteen have committed receipts from 2026-09-04. The thirteenth is a call this account placed outside the receipted set, and it is counted here because the period total is what the account was charged, not what the repository can show.
what_it_does_not_support: That $0.05 is CALL-E's price. CALL-E publishes no per-call price and this is one account's billing readout, on hackathon credit, in one month.

That the price is per call rather than per minute. Every observed call is under two minutes, so a flat $0.05 a call and a per-minute price rounded up to a two-minute minimum produce the same thirteen rows. Distinguishing them needs one call over two minutes, and this account has none.
That the price holds at volume, in another country, or outside a credit grant. Every row read IN, and the account was funded by a $1.00 top-up and a hackathon credit.
why_it_is_here: The entry published a ceiling for months and said, correctly, that no saving could be claimed because CALL-E publishes no price. A ceiling with no price beside it is a number a buyer cannot use. This is the price side, measured rather than assumed, with the three things it cannot tell anybody written down next to it.
